title: Two Lions Hunted Railway Workers for 9 Months. Their Teeth Hold a Clue

scenes.text: In 1898, two lions hunted people for nine months.
They were big, maneless males, and they took workers building a railway bridge over the Tsavo River in Kenya.
Stories from the time claimed 135 victims. Later analysis of the lions' remains put the number nearer 35.
Why people? The lions ended up in Chicago's Field Museum, and their teeth were badly damaged. Hunting big, struggling prey may simply have hurt.
In 2024, scientists pulled hairs from inside those broken teeth and read the DNA. Giraffe, zebra, wildebeest, oryx, waterbuck. And human.
A toothache may have helped turn two lions into man-eaters.

description:
In 1898 two maneless male lions preyed on workers building a railway bridge over the Tsavo River in Kenya for nine months, until the project's engineer, John Henry Patterson, shot them.
Accounts from the time claimed up to 135 victims; an isotope study of the remains pointed to around 35. Both lions had damaged teeth, one leading idea for why they turned to people, and in 2024 DNA from hairs lodged in those teeth identified giraffe, human, oryx, waterbuck, wildebeest and zebra.
Toothache, hunger, or habit: what do you think drove them?
subject: maneless male lion
first_comment: The hair DNA showed the pair had eaten at least two giraffes, and no buffalo at all. Which true predator story should we tell next?
